title: Career Psychology Digest — Motivation & Engagement — 2026-11-02

studies.title: Your boss trusts you less when you use AI — unless the company has told you to
studies.paper_title: Psychological Reactions to Subordinates’ LLM Use at Work
studies.the_study: Across six studies — five incentivized economic games plus one field study with academic supervisors — researchers tested how a subordinate's use of large language models changes a supervisor's trust in them. Using LLM-generated output reduced supervisory trust compared with doing the work yourself, though it was still trusted more than plagiarized work, and the trust penalty flowed through to lower ratings of performance, citizenship behavior and promotability. The only boundary condition that mattered was organizational policy: when the organization explicitly encouraged LLM use, the trust penalty disappeared, while task criticality and the supervisor's own AI experience made no reliable difference. In the field study, the broader a subordinate's LLM use, the less their supervisor trusted them.
studies.why_it_matters: Many employees are quietly using AI tools with no formal guidance, and this evidence suggests the ambiguity itself is costly — the same AI use is penalized under silence and forgiven under an explicit green light.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers who want AI adoption may need to say so out loud and in writing: in these studies a stated policy of encouragement was the one thing that neutralized the trust penalty. Employees can test whether disclosing AI use alongside a visible account of their own contribution protects their standing, bearing in mind that most of this evidence comes from controlled games rather than ongoing workplace relationships.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It's a window into a new kind of workplace etiquette problem: AI help sits somewhere between honest effort and cheating in the eyes of the person evaluating you, and the rules are mostly unwritten.
studies.caveats: Five of the six studies are incentivized economic games rather than real work decisions; the field study is confined to academic supervisors; downstream outcomes such as promotability are perceptions, not actual promotion records.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (six studies, five incentivized games plus academic field study), the trust ordering (own work > LLM > plagiarism), the policy-only moderation, the downstream perceptual outcomes and the Study 6 breadth effect all match the abstract. Caveats correctly note the artificial settings and that promotability is a perception.

studies.title: Bossing people around feels good and bad at the same time — for the boss
studies.paper_title: Feeling proud but guilty? Unpacking the paradoxical nature of authoritarian leadership behavior on leaders themselves
studies.the_study: Researchers used experience sampling to collect 743 daily observations from 88 supervisors, tracking their authoritarian leadership behavior and their own emotions and energy. On days when leaders behaved more authoritatively, they felt both more pride and more guilt. Pride fed into higher work engagement that day, while guilt fed into greater emotional exhaustion — and the pride pathway was stronger for leaders scoring high on Machiavellianism.
studies.why_it_matters: It helps explain why heavy-handed leadership persists despite its known costs to subordinates: it delivers an immediate psychological reward to the leader, even while quietly draining them.
studies.story_angle_primary: Leaders who notice a buzz after a day of laying down the law may be reading it as effectiveness; this study suggests tracking your own guilt and end-of-day exhaustion is a better signal. Managers could use the daily-diary logic themselves — note what you did and how depleted you feel that evening — to see whether a controlling style is self-reinforcing.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who has watched a domineering manager and wondered how they live with themselves: the data suggest they often don't, entirely — the guilt shows up the same day, as fatigue.
studies.caveats: Self-report from leaders only, so subordinate experience isn't measured; 88 supervisors is a modest sample; day-level associations within a short window can't prove the behavior causes the emotion rather than the reverse; study context and country not fully specified.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (743 observations, 88 supervisors), ESM design, dual pride/guilt pathways and the Machiavellianism moderator are all reported correctly; one loose word choice swaps the studied construct's name.

studies.title: Toxic workplaces don't just make work unpleasant — they make it feel pointless
studies.paper_title: Meaningful and meaningless work under destructive organisational context
studies.the_study: Two Polish employee samples tested how a destructive organizational context — a composite of harmful workplace conditions — relates to experiences of meaningful and meaningless work. Study 1 used a three-wave design with 1,966 employees and autoregressive controls, finding that a destructive context predicted later frustration of basic psychological needs, which in turn predicted lower meaningful work and higher meaningless work. Study 2 (N=386, two waves) found that grit buffered the link between a destructive context and need frustration, while a job growth mindset weakened the link between need frustration and loss of meaning.
studies.why_it_matters: Meaning at work is often treated as something individuals cultivate, but this large longitudinal study locates its destruction in the organizational environment — and shows the damage runs through thwarted autonomy, competence and belonging.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers chasing engagement through purpose statements may be fixing the wrong end of the chain; the evidence points to removing the destructive conditions that frustrate basic needs. The buffering role of growth mindset is worth watching, but it is a shock absorber, not a substitute for repair.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If your job has started to feel meaningless, this research suggests looking at the environment rather than assuming you've lost your passion — and that people who see their abilities as developable seem to hold onto meaning longer in bad conditions.
studies.caveats: All self-report, so predictors and outcomes share a source; Polish samples only; Study 2 is two-wave with a smaller N; observational design, so causal claims remain tentative despite autoregressive controls.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes, wave structure, the need-frustration mechanism and both moderators (grit on the ODC–NF link, growth mindset on the NF–meaning links) match the abstract. The only slippage is causal framing in "Why it matters," which sits awkwardly beside the digest's own causality caveat.

studies.title: In a 'masculinity contest' workplace, being good at the job won't save you — being connected might
studies.paper_title: Masculinity contest cultures and job satisfaction: better to be competent or embedded?
studies.the_study: Using a three-timepoint survey of 408 full-time employed adults, researchers examined when masculinity contest culture — workplace norms around toughness, competition and never showing weakness — hurts job satisfaction most. The negative link was strongest among men who felt socially unembedded at work, and essentially vanished for men who felt well connected. For women, the relationship was consistently negative except at the very lowest levels of embeddedness. Crucially, feeling competent at one's actual job tasks offered no protection at all.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that in hyper-competitive cultures, survival depends on social standing rather than performance — a dynamic that quietly disadvantages anyone outside the inner circle, regardless of how well they do the work.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers who believe a competitive culture is a meritocracy should take note: in this sample, in-role competence provided zero buffer against its costs, while social embeddedness did. Audit whether informal networks, not output, are determining who thrives.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For employees deciding whether to stay in a cutthroat workplace, the finding reframes a common piece of advice — 'just do great work and you'll be fine' — as insufficient, especially for women, for whom even strong connections didn't neutralize the effect.
studies.caveats: Self-report survey across three waves, so causality is not established; a general sample of employed adults rather than a specific organization or industry; moderation effects at the extremes of a scale should be interpreted cautiously.
studies.verdict_notes: The three-timepoint design, N = 408, the gendered embeddedness moderation pattern and the null for in-role competence are reported faithfully. The framing drifts from the single measured outcome (job satisfaction) to career survival and performance, and treats a self-perception measure as actual job competence.

studies.title: What your resting heart rate says about how well you're working
studies.paper_title: The within‐person relationship of allostasis and allostatic load with job performance
studies.the_study: Two longitudinal multilevel studies tested whether heart rate and heart rate variability track job performance within the same person over time. In Study 1, 167–331 participants took repeated resting measurements over four weeks (509–1,001 observations) alongside self- and peer/supervisor-rated performance; in Study 2, a handful of counselors measured heart rate before sessions that clients then rated. When the physiological readings reflected accumulated strain, lower resting heart rate and higher heart rate variability predicted better performance; when they reflected short-term activation before a task, the pattern partly reversed.
studies.why_it_matters: As wearables enter the workplace, this is a caution that the same biometric number can mean opposite things depending on when it is taken — accumulated burnout or useful pre-task arousal.
studies.story_angle_primary: Any employer or coach tempted to read wearable data as a productivity dashboard should note that context of measurement flips the interpretation; at minimum, resting and pre-task readings must be treated as different signals. Individuals can use the within-person logic privately: compare yourself to your own baseline, not to colleagues.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It offers a physiological account of something people sense anyway — that chronic strain shows up in the body weeks before it shows up in output, while a pre-meeting surge of arousal can actually help.
studies.caveats: Study 2 has only 11–15 counselors and under 100 sessions; performance is partly self-rated; correlational within-person design cannot show that improving cardiac indicators would improve performance; measurement-interpretation scheme is the authors' own classification.
studies.verdict_notes: Study 1 and Study 2 sample ranges, observation counts, rating sources and the core "same indicator, opposite meaning" conclusion are accurate, as are the caveats. One general-reader line asserts a time lag the study did not test.

studies.title: Showing what you actually feel at work predicts higher engagement a month later
studies.paper_title: Does expressing genuine emotions foster engagement? A within-person longitudinal study
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 1,033 Turkish white-collar employees across three monthly surveys and used a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, which separates stable personality-like differences between people from month-to-month fluctuations within the same person. In months when employees expressed their genuine emotions more than was typical for them — rather than masking or faking feelings — they reported higher work engagement the following month. The reverse path did not hold: being more engaged did not predict more authentic expression later. Employees who habitually expressed genuine emotions also tended to be more engaged overall.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that the energy employees bring to their work is partly downstream of whether they are allowed to stop performing emotions they do not feel, making display rules and "professionalism" norms an engagement lever rather than a cosmetic one.
studies.story_angle_primary: Managers can audit where their team's unwritten display rules force chronic emotional masking — mandatory cheerfulness in client calls, suppressing frustration in meetings — and whether they personally react badly when someone voices genuine feeling. The authors are explicit that the flip side, compulsory emotional disclosure, is not the remedy; the study points to removing pressure to fake, not to requiring confession.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who ends the week drained without an obvious reason: the monthly rhythm in this data suggests the effort of pretending at work may be quietly feeding into how engaged you feel weeks later, not just how tired you are that afternoon.
studies.caveats: Self-report only, with both the predictor and the outcome coming from the same employees, so common-method bias is possible; the design is a within-person panel rather than an experiment, so causality remains inferential; monthly intervals may miss faster emotional dynamics; single country (Turkey) and white-collar workers only.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (1,033 Turkish white-collar employees, three monthly waves), RI-CLPM description, the supported within-person path, the unsupported reverse path, the between-person association and the authors' caution against compulsory disclosure are all rendered correctly, with appropriate caveats.

studies.title: Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing
studies.paper_title: HRM practices and managerial evaluation in the future of work: evidence from non-standard employment
studies.the_study: Using a paired-match design, researchers collected data from 489 respondents in China — freelancers and the managers who worked with them — to test how an organization's HR practices toward freelancers shape managers' willingness to recommend them and endorse freelance work generally. Freelancers' performance, work satisfaction and (lack of) counterproductive behavior mediated the link between supportive HR practices and managerial acceptance. Organizational commitment and knowledge transfer did not mediate the relationship at all.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests managers apply a visibly different yardstick to non-standard workers: observable results count, while the relational signals that traditionally earn employees goodwill — loyalty, sharing expertise with the team — do not appear to move the needle.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your organization is scaling up freelance talent, the study implies that investing HR support in freelancers' performance conditions and satisfaction is what converts into managerial buy-in — and raises an uncomfortable question worth testing internally: are your managers crediting contractors for the integration work they do, or only for deliverables?
studies.story_angle_secondary: For independent workers, this is a reminder that the unpaid relationship-building many freelancers do to feel part of a team may not be what gets them recommended for the next contract — though it may still be what makes the work bearable.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey analyzed with PLS-SEM, so no causal inference; results are essentially a set of significant and non-significant paths in a structural model; single country (China) and knowledge-based freelance work; the measures of HR practices and managerial acceptance are newly created for this study and not yet widely validated.
studies.verdict_notes: The 489-respondent paired-match Chinese sample, the three significant mediators, the two null mediators and the new scales all match the abstract; two small points of wording/inference go slightly beyond it.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- The "leader behavior rebounds on the leader" thread holds for a second run. "Bossing people around feels good and bad at the same time — for the boss" (W7220455658) reproduces almost exactly the dual-path structure found in "Constantly scanning for problems makes leaders feel impactful — and depleted at the same time" (W7213501285): one pathway feeds the leader's engagement, a parallel one drains them. Pride/engagement versus guilt/exhaustion is now a second instance of the same mechanism, alongside the motive-dependent effects in "When the boss brags about being swamped" (W7202354404).
- Competence keeps failing as protection. "In a 'masculinity contest' workplace, being good at the job won't save you" (W7224327719) finds in-role competence offered zero buffer while social embeddedness did — the same shape as "Politically skilled employees aren't spared abusive bosses — their extra effort is what protects them" (W7172502435), where task performance did not shield employees, and as "Meta-analysis: workplace chameleons impress bosses more than they actually perform" (W7202110265), where social adaptability moved ratings rather than output.
- Work and the body stays on the agenda. "What your resting heart rate says about how well you're working" (W7220837475) sits directly alongside "When nursing home workers were happier at work, their blood showed less inflammation" (W7202070440), both using within-person designs on physiological markers — though the new study runs the arrow the other way, treating physiology as a predictor of performance rather than a consequence of job satisfaction.

**Advances**
- Within-person engagement research moves from days to months and gains a directional test. "Engagement is a daily state — and assertiveness on the day predicts it" (W7214632122) established that engagement fluctuates within the person; "Showing what you actually feel at work predicts higher engagement a month later" (W7220736490) extends this with a random-intercept cross-lagged model on 1,033 employees, separating stable differences from fluctuation and showing the reverse path does not hold. That is a methodologically stronger claim than last run's 95-person diary study.
- The non-standard workforce thread deepens. "Being bossed by an algorithm may actually help gig workers switch off at home" (W7204867954) looked at how platform work feels from the inside; "Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing" (W7213352600) adds the evaluator's side — how the organization decides whether a contingent worker is worth keeping.

**Counterpoints**
- The two batches now disagree about what earns standing, and the split tracks employment status. For employees, relational and attitudinal signals mattered more than output — early commitment predicted scarce leadership posts beyond performance scores in "Cadets who were happy at work two years earlier were likelier to win scarce leadership posts" (W7212286790), and discretionary citizenship, not task performance, protected people in W7172502435. For freelancers in W7213352600, exactly the reverse: organizational commitment and knowledge transfer mediated nothing, and only performance, satisfaction and the absence of counterproductive behavior moved managerial acceptance.
- "Toxic workplaces don't just make work unpleasant — they make it feel pointless" (W7223396210) is a useful brake on "A short video and a writing exercise cut employee exhaustion two weeks later" (W7215081402). Grit and growth mindset buffered the damage but did not remove it; the new study locates the cause squarely in the organizational environment, which reframes mindset interventions as shock absorbers rather than repairs.
- W7220736490 also complicates W7202110265: reading the room and adjusting your behavior may raise how supervisors rate you, but chronic masking of genuine emotion predicted lower engagement a month later. Style has a private cost.

**New themes**
- Generative AI enters this topic for the first time with "Your boss trusts you less when you use AI — unless the company has told you to" (W7214926983). Nothing in the previous digest addressed AI tool use, disclosure or policy.
- Gendered workplace culture as a lived day-to-day condition (W7224327719) is new; last run's gender material was about measurement and selection design (W7207756322) and women's definitions of career success (W7208791578), not about norms of toughness inside teams.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch show that what determines a worker's standing is increasingly a set of rules nobody has written down. Supervisors penalized subordinates' AI use with lower trust, performance and promotability ratings — and the penalty vanished only when the organization had explicitly said AI was encouraged ("Your boss trusts you less when you use AI," W7214926983); competence at the actual job bought no protection in competitive cultures while informal social connection did ("In a 'masculinity contest' workplace, being good at the job won't save you," W7224327719); freelancers' loyalty and knowledge sharing counted for nothing with the managers evaluating them, only deliverables did ("Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing," W7213352600); and unwritten display rules requiring people to fake feelings predicted lower engagement a month later ("Showing what you actually feel at work predicts higher engagement," W7220736490). Across all four, the gap between the formal criteria and the operative ones is where careers are quietly decided.

**Why pitch this now:** Most organizations have rolled out AI tools faster than they have written AI policies, and are simultaneously running larger contingent workforces — two situations in which employees are being judged against standards their employer has never stated out loud, and where the AI evidence suggests the written policy is the cheap, specific fix.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the cost of workplace ambiguity — why the absence of an explicit rule does not mean neutrality but defaults judgment to trust, social standing and gut feel, and what employers and workers can actually do about it. Fits a business/management readership auditing its own policies, and general-interest readers who have intuited this but never seen it measured.

**Potential headlines:**
- Workplaces Run on Rules Nobody Wrote Down
- Being Good at Your Job Is the Weakest Protection You Have
- Nobody Told You How Your Company Feels About AI, and You're Already Paying for It

**Potential outlets:**
- **Harvard Business Review** — the AI finding converts into a direct executive prescription (write the policy, say it out loud), which is squarely their register for a research-backed piece.
- **Fast Company** — covers both AI adoption inside companies and the freelance economy; this pitch joins the two under one argument about unstated evaluation criteria.
- **The Atlantic** — has long run on the social machinery of offices; the masculinity-contest and emotional-masking evidence gives an empirical spine to a story about informal status rules.
- **Business Insider** — large readership of workers currently using AI tools without guidance and wondering whether to disclose it; the trust-penalty data answers a question they are actively asking.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Your boss trusts you less when you use AI — unless the company has told you to (Work ID W7214926983):** Secret AI use carries a measurable trust and promotability penalty that an explicit company green light erases — the most actionable AI-at-work finding of the quarter, for a workplace news brief and a follow-up manager-audience column on writing an AI policy.
- **Bossing people around feels good and bad at the same time — for the boss (Work ID W7220455658):** Why heavy-handed management persists — it delivers same-day pride and engagement to the leader while quietly loading guilt and exhaustion, more so for high-Machiavellian leaders; for a leadership column or a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet.
- **Toxic workplaces don't just make work unpleasant — they make it feel pointless (Work ID W7223396210):** Nearly 2,000 employees tracked over three waves show meaninglessness is manufactured by the environment, not lost passion — a direct rebuttal to purpose-statement engagement strategy, for an HR/management explainer, with a softer "it's not you, it's the job" version for a women's/lifestyle careers section.
- **In a 'masculinity contest' workplace, being good at the job won't save you (Work ID W7224327719):** Competence bought no protection and connections did — except for women, for whom even strong connections didn't fully neutralize the cost; a strong workplace-culture and gender piece for a general-interest or women's/lifestyle outlet, and a culture-audit column for managers.
- **What your resting heart rate says about how well you're working (Work ID W7220837475):** The same wearable number means opposite things depending on when it's taken — a timely caution for employers eyeing biometric productivity dashboards, for a future-of-work or workplace-tech brief.
- **Showing what you actually feel at work predicts higher engagement a month later (Work ID W7220736490):** Mandatory cheerfulness is an engagement problem, not a cosmetic one — with the authors' own caveat that forced disclosure is not the remedy; for a career-advice column or a work-psychology explainer in a general-interest or lifestyle outlet.
- **Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing (Work ID W7213352600):** Contractors' unpaid relationship-building doesn't convert into recommendations — only deliverables do; a sharp piece for freelancers and for companies scaling contingent talent, for a careers column or a hiring/HR explainer.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Career Psychology Digest — Motivation & Engagement — 2026-11-02
**Checked:** 2026-11-02 | **Studies reviewed:** 7
**Primary audience:** working professionals and managers | **Secondary audience:** general readers

---

### Study 1: Your boss trusts you less when you use AI — unless the company has told you to
**Work ID:** W7214926983 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: Bossing people around feels good and bad at the same time — for the boss
**Work ID:** W7220455658 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Authoritatively" vs. authoritarian leadership** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "On days when leaders behaved more authoritatively, they felt both more pride and more guilt."
- **Abstract says:** "authoritarian leadership can simultaneously elicit feelings of pride and guilt in leaders"
- **Problem:** "Authoritative" and "authoritarian" are distinct leadership constructs; using the former risks readers thinking the study is about confident, expert-based leadership rather than controlling, domineering behavior.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "On days when leaders behaved more authoritarianly" or "On days with more authoritarian leadership behavior"."

### Study 3: Toxic workplaces don't just make work unpleasant — they make it feel pointless
**Work ID:** W7223396210 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal framing beyond "associated with"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this large longitudinal study locates its destruction in the organizational environment — and shows the damage runs through thwarted autonomy, competence and belonging"
- **Abstract says:** "ODC was prospectively associated with higher NF, which was associated with lower meaningful work and higher MLW; both longitudinal indirect associations were significant."
- **Problem:** The abstract consistently uses "associated" language for an observational panel design; "locates its destruction" and "shows the damage runs through" assert causation and mechanism more firmly than the evidence allows, partly contradicting the digest's own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "links lower meaning to the organizational environment" and "the association appears to run through frustrated needs for autonomy, competence and belonging.""

### Study 4: In a 'masculinity contest' workplace, being good at the job won't save you — being connected might
**Work ID:** W7224327719 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Outcome drift from job satisfaction to "survival" and "thriving"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It suggests that in hyper-competitive cultures, survival depends on social standing rather than performance"
- **Abstract says:** "the relationship between MCC and job satisfaction is moderated by gender... there were no moderation effects associated with perceived in-role competence"
- **Problem:** The only outcome in the abstract is job satisfaction. Nothing in the study measures whether people survive, advance or thrive, so "survival depends on social standing" (and the angle's "who thrives") overstates what was tested.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as "job satisfaction in hyper-competitive cultures tracks social connectedness rather than felt competence" and change "who thrives" to "who stays satisfied"."

**Issue B. Perceived competence presented as actual job competence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Crucially, feeling competent at one's actual job tasks offered no protection at all."
- **Abstract says:** "there were no moderation effects associated with perceived in-role competence, potentially reflecting that in-role performance may not buffer employees against the potential harms of MCC environments"
- **Problem:** The measure is perceived in-role competence, and the abstract hedges the inference with "potentially"; the headline's "being good at the job" and the flat "no protection at all" read as a test of real performance.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "employees' own sense of being good at their job tasks showed no buffering effect" and keep the authors' hedge."

### Study 5: What your resting heart rate says about how well you're working
**Work ID:** W7220837475 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported temporal claim** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "chronic strain shows up in the body weeks before it shows up in output"
- **Abstract says:** "When HR/HRV were interpreted as secondary outcomes, lower HR, lower LFHF, and higher HRV predicted better job performance... the same physiological indicators may show opposite relationships with performance depending on the timing and context of measurement."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports within-person associations between physiological indicators and performance ratings; it does not establish that bodily signs of strain precede performance decline by weeks.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "accumulated strain registers in resting cardiac measures that track alongside weaker performance, while a pre-task surge of arousal can go with better performance.""

### Study 6: Showing what you actually feel at work predicts higher engagement a month later
**Work ID:** W7220736490 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing
**Work ID:** W7213352600 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Composition of the paired sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "researchers collected data from 489 respondents in China — freelancers and the managers who worked with them"
- **Abstract says:** "We employed paired-match approach to collect data from 489 respondents."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not specify who made up the matched pairs; the freelancer–manager pairing is a reasonable inference but is not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "489 respondents in China using a paired-match design" or attribute the pairing explicitly as an inference."

**Issue B. "Did not mediate at all" overstates a null result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Organizational commitment and knowledge transfer did not mediate the relationship at all."
- **Abstract says:** "knowledge transfer and integration and organizational commitment do not significantly mediate this relationship"
- **Problem:** A non-significant path is not evidence of zero effect; "at all" converts a null finding into a proven absence.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "Organizational commitment and knowledge transfer showed no significant mediating effect.""

Caveats correctly note the artificial settings and that promotability is a perception. |

The only slippage is causal framing in "Why it matters," which sits awkwardly beside the digest's own causality caveat. |

The framing drifts from the single measured outcome (job satisfaction) to career survival and performance, and treats a self-perception measure as actual job competence. |
| 5 | What your resting heart rate says about how well you're working | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study 1 and Study 2 sample ranges, observation counts, rating sources and the core "same indicator, opposite meaning" conclusion are accurate, as are the caveats. One general-reader line asserts a time lag the study did not test. |

| 7 | Managers judge freelancers on output, not loyalty or knowledge sharing | ⚠️ Minor issues | The 489-respondent paired-match Chinese sample, the three significant mediators, the two null mediators and the new scales all match the abstract; two small points of wording/inference go slightly beyond it. |
